title: Taking away: displacement and relative velocity

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is your own arrow turned round and added to the bank and the second vessel, so each slides past at its velocity minus yours, when you switch to "seen from the boat".
interactive.title: The boat and the stream
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Two scenes share these screens. The first is a chart grid with the origin marked. Arrows run from the origin to points. A readout gives each arrow's i and j parts. To take b away from a, turn b round and add it nose to tail. The same answer is also drawn tail to tail. It runs from the nose of b to the nose of a. Go out along b, then along that arrow, and you land on a. The second scene is a stretch of water between two banks, seen from above. The stream's arrow runs along the banks. The boat's arrow is its heading and speed through the water. You can drag either arrow. Each second the boat makes its own step through the water. The water carries it on by the stream's step. So its track over the ground runs along the sum of the two arrows. A ghost boat follows that track. A target on the far bank marks where you want to land. A switch shows the scene from the boat. There, your own arrow is turned round and added to everything. So your boat sits still. The bank slides past backwards. A second vessel moves along its velocity minus yours. The screens run like this. First, a = 5i + 2j and b = 1i + 3j, with a − b drawn both ways. A puzzle takes 2i − 1j away from 3i + 4j. Buoys A and B sit at 1i + 2j and 6i + 5j km, with the move between them. A puzzle asks for the move from P, 4i − 1j, to Q, −2i + 3j. Points A, B and C at 1i + 1j, 3i + 2j and 7i + 4j lie on one line. A puzzle picks the point in line with A and B. The boat heads across at 4 m/s in a 3 m/s stream. Then it aims off to land opposite. A puzzle has a 5 m/s boat crossing straight over a 3 m/s stream. Then the scene is seen from the boat. You make 6i knots, and a second vessel makes 8j knots. A puzzle has vessels at 4i + 3j and −2i + 3j knots. Two mixed puzzles end it. In one, two vessels meet head-on at 12 knots each. In the other, a boat points straight at a target 40 m across. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn too. You can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The stream is drawn at one speed everywhere. It is steady in time, too. A real river runs faster mid-channel. A tidal stream changes hour by hour. The boat's speed through the water is held fixed. No wind pushes it sideways. Turns take no time. Everything lies flat on the page. Vectors in 3-D take away the same way, with their k parts too. Taking velocities away like this holds at everyday speeds. Close to the speed of light, it needs relativity instead. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
Taking a vector away means adding its reverse. To work out a − b, turn b round and add it nose to tail.[^1] Here is why. The answer a − b is the arrow you add to b to reach a. Take a = 5i + 2j and b = 1i + 3j. Turned round, b is −1i − 3j. Add it part by part. Across, 5 − 1 = 4. Up, 2 − 3 = −1. So a − b = 4i − 1j. Check it by adding b back on. Add 1i + 3j to 4i − 1j and you get 5i + 2j. That is a. Now draw a and b from the same tail. Go out along b, then along a − b. You land on a's nose. So a − b runs from b's nose to a's nose. Adding them instead gives 6i + 5j. That arrow points somewhere else.

A move from one point to another is a [[displacement]]. Draw an arrow from the origin to buoy A. Call it a. It is A's [[position vector]]. Draw another to buoy B, and call that one b. Go out along a, then make the move from A to B. You land on B. So a + AB = b. Take a away from both sides. That leaves AB = b − a. A displacement is where you end minus where you started.[^2] Say A sits at 1i + 2j km and B at 6i + 5j km. Then AB = 5i + 3j km. BA is the same move backwards, −5i − 3j km. Taking away also shows when three points lie on one line. Take A, B and C at 1i + 1j, 3i + 2j and 7i + 4j. AB = 2i + 1j. BC = 4i + 2j. That is 2 × AB. So the two steps point the same way. Parallel steps alone could sit on two separate lines. These two share B. So they lie on one line. The three points are [[collinear]].

Velocities add and take away the same way. A boat's heading and speed through the water make one velocity. The stream moves the water itself. Each second, the boat makes its own step through the water. The water carries it on by the stream's step. Those steps add nose to tail. So the boat's velocity over the ground is the sum of the two. Say you head straight across at 4 m/s in a 3 m/s stream. The two arrows meet at a right angle. So over the ground you make √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s. Your track runs 36.87° downstream of your heading. To land straight opposite, aim upstream. The heading you need is the track you want minus the stream. Turn until your upstream part is 3 m/s. That cancels the stream. Your heading is now the long side of a right triangle. Its short sides are the upstream part and the across part. So your across part is √(4² − 3²) = 2.65 m/s. The heading is 48.59° upstream of straight across.

Now look from your own boat. To you, the boat sits still. Adding the reverse of your velocity makes it zero. You add that reverse to everything you watch. That keeps the differences between them the same. So the bank slides past at minus your velocity. Another vessel seems to move at its velocity minus yours. That is its [[relative velocity]].[^3] Measure both velocities over the ground. Say you make 6i knots, due east. A second vessel makes 8j knots, due north. Seen from you, it moves at 8j − 6i = −6i + 8j. Its size is √(6² + 8²) = 10 knots. Adding them instead gives 6i + 8j. That arrow leans east, not west.

A turbine blade works the same way. The blade is moving, so the steam meets it at the steam's velocity minus the blade's. Marine engineers draw these velocity diagrams at the blade's inlet and outlet.[^4]

**Taking a vector away means adding its reverse. A displacement is end minus start. A relative velocity is the other's velocity minus yours.**

analogy.text: Your voltmeter takes away in the same way. Put the red lead on B and the black lead on A. It reads the potential at B minus the potential at A. That is the same order as the move from A to B. Swap the leads and the same size comes up with a minus sign. A displacement behaves like that. AB is b − a. BA is the same move backwards. The reading is a difference, not a sum.
analogy.breaks: A potential is a plain number. So the difference is a plain number too. A displacement has a direction. So you take away the across parts and the up parts separately. The answer is an arrow.

practice.text:
- Settle the order first. The other vessel relative to you is the other's velocity minus yours. The move from A to B is b − a.
- Write both vectors as i and j parts. Measure both against the same thing. Use both over the ground, or both through the water.
- Turn round the one you take away. Flip the sign of every part.
- Add part by part.
- Sketch it tail to tail. The answer runs from the nose of the one you took away to the nose of the other.
- Check it by adding your answer back on. You should get the first vector again.

**Rule of thumb:** End minus start, and theirs minus yours. Steam meeting a moving turbine blade works the same way. The blade meets the steam's velocity minus its own.

**Worked example:** Say you want to cross a 200 m channel straight over. Your boat makes 2.5 m/s through the water. The stream runs at 1.5 m/s. Aim upstream until your upstream part is 1.5 m/s. Your across part is √(2.5² − 1.5²) = 2 m/s. The heading is sin⁻¹(1.5 ÷ 2.5) = 36.87° upstream of straight across. The crossing takes 200 ÷ 2 = 100 s. Now say you pointed straight across instead. You would cross in 200 ÷ 2.5 = 80 s. In that time the stream carries you 1.5 × 80 = 120 m downstream.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding when you mean to take away. Two vessels head-on at 12 knots each close at 24 knots, not 0.
- Getting the order backwards. b − a and a − b are the same size and point opposite ways.
- Flipping the sign of only some of the parts.
- Pointing straight at the target. The stream carries you downstream of it.
- Mixing what you measure against. One velocity over the ground and the other through the water give an answer that means nothing.
- Calling points collinear because two steps are parallel. The steps must share a point too.
- Joining the dots on a course to steer. A line from the end of the stream's arrow straight to the target is the wrong heading. From the end of the stream's arrow, swing your speed through the water until it meets the line to the target.[^5]
